title: Pip and the Weather Balloon
sum: The Ridgeview School science club builds a foam box named Pip, sends it 31 kilometers up under a weather balloon, and follows the numbers to bring it and its data home.

cast.d: an eleven-year-old girl in the science club who keeps the launch log and loves exact words
cast.look: an eleven-year-old girl with a long dark braid, a purple hoodie and a pencil behind her ear

cast.d: a twelve-year-old boy in the science club who does sums in his head and worries out loud
cast.look: a twelve-year-old boy with short black hair, round glasses and an orange soccer jersey

cast.d: an eleven-year-old boy in the science club who builds things and draws on everything
cast.look: an eleven-year-old boy with messy black hair, a green jacket covered in marker doodles and a roll of silver tape on his wrist

cast.d: the science teacher who runs the club, calm and a little dry
cast.look: a tall woman with dark brown skin, short gray-streaked hair, a denim jacket and a clipboard

cast.d: a sheep farmer east of town whose dog finds Pip
cast.look: an older woman with a gray bun, tall rubber boots and a red flannel shirt
a black-and-white border collie with one ear up and one ear down

cast.d: the club's foam box that rides under the balloon
cast.look: a white foam box the size of a shoebox, with a black marker penguin on one side and a label taped to the lid
a palm-sized white plastic astronaut with a waffle pattern on his helmet

p: The box from the balloon company was smaller than a shoebox, which was not what Omar had pictured at all. Jun sniffed the packing tape while Omar shook the box next to his ear and frowned. “That's it? I thought a weather balloon would be enormous, like something in a parade.”

Their teacher, Ms. Oduya, slit the tape with her car key and lifted out a floppy white bundle that smelled like new rubber gloves. Held up by one end, it drooped toward the floor like a sleeping jellyfish. “It will be enormous,” she said, “about two meters wide on launch day, and much bigger by the time it reaches the top.”

The Ridgeview School science club had three weeks to get ready. Their balloon would carry a small box about 30 kilometers up, nearly three times as high as a passenger jet flies. Inside the box would ride a camera, a tracker and a data logger to record the temperature and air pressure every minute. Rosa wrote LAUNCH LOG across the first page of a new notebook and underlined it twice.

Rosa asked, “How cold does it get up there?” Their teacher drew a tall mountain on the whiteboard with snow on its peak. “For the first ten kilometers or so, the air gets about 6.5 degrees colder for every kilometer you climb,” she said. “That's why high mountains keep their snow in July.”

Omar grabbed Rosa's pencil and worked it out in the corner of her page, starting from the forecast of 15 °C for launch day. Ten kilometers up, the air would be 6.5 × 10 degrees colder, which came to 65 degrees. He looked up with wide eyes and said, “That's fifty below zero!”

“Fifty below,” said their teacher, “and batteries hate the cold.” She set two small cameras on the table, one for the flight and one spare, both the same model. “Whatever box we build has to keep these warm enough to work.”

Jun already had a plan, and it was a shoebox with a neat round hole cut in one end for the lens. Rosa wanted the foam box from the supply closet instead, since it was almost the same size. “Foam is lighter,” she said. “Cardboard is tougher,” said Jun, and they both turned to their teacher.

“Test them both,” she said. “Change one thing, and keep everything else the same.” So both cameras got fully charged batteries and were set to record, and then one went into the shoebox while the other went into the foam box.

The two boxes sat side by side on one shelf of the cafeteria's walk-in freezer, at 18 degrees below zero. “If a camera quits at minus eighteen, it will quit up there,” their teacher said as the heavy door shut with a whump. Omar set a timer for 40 minutes and then checked it every two minutes, which Rosa wrote down in the log.

When the timer finally beeped, they hurried back, and cold air rolled out around their ankles. The camera in the shoebox was as cold as an ice cube tray, and its screen stayed black even when Jun pressed the power button. Then Rosa pulled the lid off the foam box and found a tiny red light still blinking.

Jun looked from one camera to the other. “How can that be, when the cameras are twins?” “Foam is full of tiny bubbles of trapped air, and trapped air is slow to carry heat away,” their teacher said as she tapped the white lid. “The camera makes a little warmth while it's recording, and the foam keeps that warmth in, like a winter jacket.”

Rosa wrote “Test: foam good” in the log and then frowned at it, because nobody reading it later would know what happened. She crossed it out and tried again: “Foam wins. The shoebox camera died after 40 minutes, but the foam box camera kept recording.”

Meanwhile, Jun uncapped a black marker and drew on the side of the foam box. First came a round belly, then two flippers and a pointy beak. “Anything that lives in the cold needs a face,” he said. Omar leaned over and asked, “Does it get a name?” Rosa already had one, and she wrote it at the bottom of the page: Pip.

art.s: In a school cafeteria, three kids crowd around a small foam box with a tiny red camera light blinking inside, while an open shoebox holding a dark camera sits beside it and cold mist drifts out of a big freezer door.

q.q: Draw the two boxes when they came out of the freezer. Show which camera still worked, and what kept it warm.
look: the shoebox camera with a black screen
the foam box camera with its red light blinking
tiny bubbles of air in the foam holding the warmth in
q.e: You drew the whole test, and why the foam won!

q.q: Rosa wrote “Foam wins” in the log. What happened in the freezer that shows she was right?
q.a: After 40 minutes in the freezer, the shoebox camera had died, but the foam box camera was still recording. Everything else was the same, so the box made the difference.
q.e: A good log backs up what it says with what really happened. Rosa's proof was the two cameras.

q.q: The air gets about 6.5 degrees colder for every kilometer up. How much colder is it 4 kilometers up?
c: 24 degrees colder
26 degrees colder
10.5 degrees colder
32.5 degrees colder
q.e: 6.5 × 4 = 26. Four kilometers up, the air is about 26 degrees colder.

p: On Tuesday afternoon, Omar marched into the science classroom with a question he had been saving all weekend. He dropped his backpack on a desk and asked, “Why does our balloon have to pop? Why can't it just keep going, all the way up into outer space?”

Ms. Oduya didn't answer right away. Instead, she opened a drawer and took out a plastic syringe with no needle, along with a bag of miniature marshmallows that made Jun sit up very straight. “They're not for eating,” she told him, “at least not yet.”

She dropped one marshmallow into the syringe and pushed the plunger down until it almost touched the marshmallow. Then she pressed her thumb over the tip and pulled the plunger back as far as it would go. The marshmallow swelled, fatter and fatter, until it was nearly twice its size. When she lifted her thumb, air rushed back in with a tiny pff, and the marshmallow shrank into a wrinkly lump.

Omar wanted to see it again, so this time Jun held the syringe and watched the marshmallow puff up inside the tube. “Air is always pressing on everything around us,” said their teacher. “When you pull the plunger back, there's less air in there to push on the marshmallow, so the tiny bubbles of air inside it push out and make it grow.”
Jun frowned at the marshmallow for a moment. “So it's like a dog pile, where the kid on the very bottom gets squished the most,” he said.

Their teacher pointed at the floor. “And all of us live at the bottom of the air,” she said. “The higher the balloon goes, the less air is piled on top of it, so it grows and grows until the rubber can't stretch any farther.” She snapped her fingers like a popping balloon, and Omar jumped.

Rosa asked, “How big does it get?” Their teacher checked the side of the balloon's box. “It's about 2 meters wide when it leaves the ground, and about 8 meters wide at the top,” she said. Omar counted by twos on his fingers until he reached eight, and his mouth fell open.

Jun couldn't imagine anything that big, so he laid the meter stick on the floor with one end against the whiteboard. Flip, flip, flip went the stick down the aisle between the desks. Rosa followed with a roll of blue tape and stuck a strip on the floor at every meter. The eighth strip landed right under the fish tank at the back wall.

The three of them stood by the fish tank and looked all the way back to the whiteboard. “Our balloon is going to be as wide as the whole science room,” Omar said. “And then it pops,” said Rosa, “and Pip falls.”

“Under a parachute,” said Ms. Oduya, and she held up a bright orange one that was not much bigger than a beach towel. “Pip will land wherever the wind takes it, maybe in a cornfield or a backyard or on somebody's roof.”

Jun frowned. “So a total stranger finds a foam box with a penguin on it and has no idea what it is.” That was how the label became Rosa's job. She worked on it that night at the kitchen table, and by bedtime it filled a whole page in tiny, neat handwriting. It began, “Dear Finder, please do not be alarmed,” and went on to describe the science club, the balloon, the data logger and the weather forecast.

Omar read it the next morning and handed it back. “Nobody's going to read all this while they're standing in a field,” he said. Rosa's ears went hot, but Jun tapped the top of the page and asked, “What do they need to know first?”

“That it's safe,” said Rosa, and she started over on a fresh card in big capital letters. HARMLESS SCIENCE PROJECT went at the very top. Under that came the club's name, then PLEASE CALL and their teacher's phone number. At the bottom, Omar made her add one more line: REWARD: COOKIES.
Jun taped the label to Pip's lid, right above the penguin's head. Their teacher read it, raised one eyebrow and asked, “Cookies?” Omar just shrugged. “I'd call.”

art.s: In a science classroom, a teacher holds up a syringe with a puffed-up marshmallow inside while three kids watch, and a line of blue tape strips runs across the floor to a fish tank at the back wall.

q.q: Draw the balloon on launch day and at the top, side by side. How many small balloons fit across the big one?
look: four small balloons fitting across the big one
q.e: Great comparing! Four launch-day balloons fit across the balloon at the top.

q.q: Why did the marshmallow grow when Ms. Oduya pulled the plunger back?
c: Less air was pushing on it
The syringe warmed it up
It soaked up extra air
Her thumb squeezed it
q.e: With less air pressing on it, the air bubbles inside pushed out. The balloon grows the same way as it rises.

q.q: Why did Rosa put HARMLESS SCIENCE PROJECT at the very top of her new label?
q.a: The first thing a finder needs to know is that the box is safe. Big, short words at the top can be read fast, even by someone standing in a field.
q.e: A good notice puts the most important words first, big and short.

p: Launch day began at 6:30 in the morning on the soccer field behind the school, where the wet grass had just been mowed. A low mist hung over everything, and the far goalposts looked gray and blurry, like a picture someone had smudged with a thumb. The flag by the gym hung straight down without a single flap. “No wind at all, which is just what we want,” said Ms. Oduya.

A tall green tank of helium stood on a cart beside a plastic tarp. Everyone pulled on gloves first, because the oil from bare skin can weaken the balloon's thin rubber. Their teacher fitted the neck of the balloon over the hose and opened the valve with a long hiss. Little by little, the floppy white bundle on the tarp began to lift its head.

It grew rounder and taller until it towered over all of them, bobbing at the end of its line. A man walking a golden retriever stopped at the fence to stare, and the dog barked at the balloon as if it were the biggest ball in the world. Jun held on with both hands and leaned back with his heels dug into the grass. “It's pulling like a dog that just saw a squirrel,” he said, and Rosa wrote that in the log, word for word.

Omar asked, “Why does it pull so hard?” “Helium is much lighter than air, so the heavier air all around squeezes in underneath the balloon and shoves it upward,” their teacher said. She pushed an invisible ball down with both hands. “It's like trying to hold a beach ball under water at the swimming pool.”

While the balloon filled, Omar weighed Pip on a kitchen scale, since the club's limit was one kilogram and a lighter box climbs faster and lands more gently. The screen said 1.06 kg, and Omar groaned. “We're six hundredths of a kilogram too heavy, which is about the weight of one egg,” he said.

Rosa looked at Omar, and Omar looked at his shoes. Then he opened Pip's lid and lifted out a small plastic astronaut with a waffle pattern on his helmet. “This is Captain Waffles,” he said, “and he has always wanted to fly.”
On his own, Captain Waffles weighed 0.04 kg, and Omar's shoulders sank as he did the subtraction in his head. “Even without him, we'd still be two hundredths of a kilogram over the limit,” he said.

Jun knelt beside the box and lifted out the spare camera, the one that had quit inside a cold shoebox during their freezer test. It weighed 0.12 kg by itself. “We only need one camera,” Jun said, and he tucked Captain Waffles back in beside the logger and pressed the lid shut.

Their teacher checked the scale and gave them a thumbs-up. By 7:40 the balloon was as wide as a car and almost glowing in the mist. Jun switched on the camera and the logger, and a tiny red light began to blink through the hole in the foam. Then Ms. Oduya tied the balloon's line to the orange parachute, and the parachute's line to Pip.
Rosa held Pip in both arms while Jun held the balloon, and Omar counted down from ten. On zero, Jun opened his hands. The line snapped tight, and Rosa let Pip go too.

The balloon shot straight up, much faster than any of them had expected, with the parachute and then Pip swinging along below it. In ten seconds it was higher than the school roof. In a minute it was only a white dot, and then the mist swallowed it and it was gone.
Omar's head was still tipped back toward the empty sky, and his mouth hung open. Rosa looked down at her notebook and wrote, “7:42 — Liftoff! Captain Waffles aboard.”

art.s: On a misty soccer field at dawn, a huge white weather balloon rises into the sky with an orange parachute and a small foam box with a penguin drawing swinging below it, while three kids in gloves watch with their heads tipped back.

q.q: Pip weighed 1.06 kg. Jun took out the spare camera, which weighed 0.12 kg. How much did Pip weigh then?
q.a: Pip weighed 0.94 kg, because 1.06 − 0.12 = 0.94. That is under the 1 kg limit, even with Captain Waffles inside.
q.e: 1.06 − 0.12 = 0.94. Pip was 0.06 kg under the limit, so Captain Waffles got to fly!

q.q: Jun said the balloon was “pulling like a dog that just saw a squirrel.” What did he mean?
c: It was pulling hard and fast
It was making a lot of noise
It was swinging side to side
It was trying to come down
q.e: A dog that spots a squirrel yanks hard on its leash. The balloon yanked hard to go up.

q.q: Draw the balloon pulling on its line. Use arrows to show the heavier air pushing it up.
look: a balloon full of light helium
arrows pushing up from the air underneath
the line pulled tight toward the sky
q.e: Your arrows show why a helium balloon rises, just like a beach ball in water!

p: At 7:49, Omar's phone buzzed with a text from Pip's tracker: 2.1 km up and climbing. He held it high so everyone could see, grinning as if he had built the tracker himself. Then the phone went quiet, and it stayed quiet for five minutes, then ten, then twenty.

“It's broken,” Omar said. “Or it fell off, or the battery died, or—” “It's just too high,” said Ms. Oduya as she rolled the empty helium tank toward her van. “The tracker sends its texts through cell towers, and the towers aim along the ground, not up at the sky. When Pip comes back down low, it'll start talking again.”

The winds high in the atmosphere were blowing east that morning, so the club piled into the van and drove east too. The van smelled like coffee and old sneakers, and nobody said very much. About 40 kilometers from school, their teacher pulled into a diner so they could wait somewhere with pancakes. Omar grabbed a paper napkin and a pen before he had even sat down.

He wanted a time, because a time was something you could wait for. Pip would pop at about 30 kilometers, and the balloon climbed about 0.3 kilometers every minute. He tried 0.3 × 100 on the napkin and got exactly 30. “So it takes around 100 minutes to reach the top,” he said. “How long does it take to come down?”

“About 35 minutes, according to the parachute chart,” said Ms. Oduya. Omar added the two times together and counted forward from 7:42, the minute Pip had lifted off. “So it lands at about 9:57,” he said, and he drew a circle around the time twice.
When the waitress came to refill the coffee, she read the napkin upside down and asked, “Rocket science?” “Balloon science,” said Jun, and she brought the whole table extra whipped cream anyway.
At 9:15 Omar found a brand-new worry and put down his fork. “When the balloon pops, Pip falls from 30 kilometers up,” he said. “What if the parachute doesn't even work up there?”

Their teacher set down her cup. “Up there, the air is so thin that the parachute has almost nothing to grab,” she said. “At first Pip will drop faster than a car on the highway.” She swooped her flat hand down toward the table and then slowed it. “Lower down, the air gets thicker, the parachute bites, and Pip slows down.”

By then Rosa had filled four pages of the log with the mist, the gloves, Captain Waffles and the waitress with her rocket science. Then their teacher's phone lit up, because the parents' group chat wanted news. “One sentence,” she said, and she slid the phone across to Rosa. “Just the big news.”

Rosa flipped back through her four pages. The waitress was funny, but she was not big news, and neither were Omar's two pancakes. Rosa typed one sentence, deleted half of it and pressed send, and a minute later Jun's dad replied with a row of tiny balloons.

At 9:57, Omar stared at the phone, and nothing happened. By 9:59 his knee was bouncing so hard that the syrup bottle began to walk across the table, and Rosa had to grab it. At 10:01 the phone buzzed so loudly that all three kids jumped in their seats.

“Pip, 2.3 km, falling,” Omar read out loud. More texts came every couple of minutes, and he read each one like a countdown as the number got smaller and smaller. The last text had no height at all, only a map pin and a road name: Varga Farm Road, 61 km east of the school.
Their teacher left money on the table and picked up her keys. “Come on,” she said, “let's go get our penguin.”

art.s: In a small-town diner booth, three kids and their teacher lean over a buzzing phone beside plates of pancakes, a syrup bottle and a paper napkin covered in numbers.

q.q: The parents wanted one sentence of big news. Which one is the best summary?
c: Pip is flying, and we're waiting east of town for it.
The waitress asked if we were doing rocket science.
Omar ate two big pancakes at the diner.
Ms. Oduya's van smells like coffee and sneakers.
q.e: A summary tells the big news. The pancakes were fun, but they weren't the big news.

q.q: Ms. Oduya said Pip would fall fast at first, then slower. Why?
q.a: Up high the air is very thin, so the parachute has almost nothing to grab and Pip falls fast. Lower down the air is thicker, so the parachute catches more air and slows Pip down.
q.e: Thick air gives a parachute something to push against. That's why Pip slowed down near the ground.

q.q: Draw a graph of Pip's height. Show about 100 minutes going up and about 35 minutes coming down.
look: a line that climbs for a long time
a top point at about 30 km
a shorter, steeper line coming down
q.e: Your graph tells Pip's whole trip in one picture!

p: The club was still ten minutes from the farm when Ms. Oduya's phone rang, and she put it on speaker. “Hello, this is Ilona Varga, out on Varga Farm Road,” said a woman's voice. “My dog found a foam box with a penguin on it, and the label says it's a harmless science project and to please call. There's also something about cookies.”

Mrs. Varga was waiting at her gate in tall rubber boots, with Pip tucked under one arm. Beside her sat Pogo, a black-and-white sheepdog who looked very pleased with himself. “He barked at your orange parachute until I came out to the sheep field,” she said as she handed Pip over. “Now, about these cookies.”

Omar held out a tin with both hands, and she took a cookie and broke off a corner for Pogo. Pip had one dent and a lot of grass stuck to its tape, but the camera and the logger inside were fine. Captain Waffles was upside down but still in one piece. Then the farmer put the kettle on and cleared a spot on her kitchen table for Jun's laptop.

The logger had taken a reading every minute of the flight, and Rosa scrolled all the way back to the beginning. Before liftoff, it had checked the air on the soccer field five times: 14.6, 15.2, 14.8, 15.4 and 15.0 degrees. She asked, “Which one of these goes in our report?”

“All of them, because we average them,” said Omar. He borrowed a pencil from the jar by the telephone and added the five numbers on the back of a seed catalog, and they came to exactly 75. He started to divide, and Pogo rested his chin on the edge of the table to watch.

Then Jun scrolled down through the flight. As Pip rose, the temperature dropped, and dropped, and kept on dropping, until at 10 kilometers up the logger said −49.6 °C. Omar sat straight up in his chair and pointed at the screen. “Three weeks ago I said it would be fifty below, and I was right!”

The coldest reading came at about 12 kilometers, where it was almost 57 degrees below zero. After that, something odd happened, because the numbers began to climb again. By the top, just over 31 kilometers up, the air had warmed to about 45 below. “But that's warmer,” Rosa said with a frown.
“So the logger broke,” said Omar, but Jun shook his head. “The sensor hung outside the box on a wire, where it could feel the real air, and I taped it on myself.”

“It's real,” said Ms. Oduya as she leaned over the screen. “High up, there's a layer of air with a gas called ozone in it. Ozone soaks up sunlight and warms the air around it, the way a black T-shirt heats up on a sunny day.”
Omar squinted at her and asked, “So it's not because Pip was closer to the sun?” “Only thirty kilometers closer,” she said, “and the sun is 150 million kilometers away.”

Rosa found the pressure column next. On the soccer field it read 1,000, but at the top it read just 10, which was only one part in a hundred. “So Pip was higher than 99 percent of all the air,” Omar said, and Rosa wrote that in the log in capital letters.

Last of all, Jun opened the camera's pictures. Most were blurry, because Pip had spun and swung the whole way up, but then one came up that made everyone stop talking. Brown fields, green fields and a few white clouds lay under a thin blue line, and above that line the sky was black.
The farmer leaned in close and asked, “Is my farm in there somewhere?” “Somewhere under that cloud,” said Jun.

art.s: At a farmhouse kitchen table, a farmer, a sheepdog, three kids and their teacher lean toward a laptop showing fields and clouds under a thin blue line and a black sky, beside a muddy foam box with a penguin drawn on it and a tin of cookies.

q.q: Draw Mrs. Varga and Pogo finding Pip in the sheep field. Give Mrs. Varga a speech bubble.
look: the penguin box and the orange parachute in the grass
a speech bubble with what Mrs. Varga might say
q.e: Your speech bubble lets us hear what Mrs. Varga was thinking!

q.q: Before liftoff, the logger read 14.6, 15.2, 14.8, 15.4 and 15.0 degrees. What was the average?
q.a: The average was 15.0 degrees. The five readings add up to 75, and 75 ÷ 5 = 15.
q.e: An average shares the total out evenly. 75 shared by 5 is 15.

q.q: Why did the air get warmer near the top of Pip's flight?
c: Ozone up there soaks up sunlight
Pip was much closer to the sun
The box warmed up the sensor
The balloon made heat when it popped
q.e: Ozone soaks up sunlight and warms the air, like a black T-shirt in the sun. Thirty kilometers closer to the sun hardly matters!

fin.q: How did Rosa's label help the club get Pip back?
fin.a: Mrs. Varga read on the label that the box was a harmless science project, so she knew it was safe to pick up. Then she called the number, and the club came to get Pip.
fin.e: Rosa's short, clear label did its job, far out in a sheep field.

fin.q: Up high, the balloon grew huge and the parachute fell fast. What one thing caused both?
c: The air up high is thin
The air up high is cold
The wind blows east
Helium is lighter than air
fin.e: Thin air pushes less on the balloon, so it grows. It also gives the parachute less to grab.
